column2: Trained horsemen, O king, surrounding great chariot-warriors, ranged in the battle and struck them with lances, darts and spears.
Some bowmen, holding back great chariot-warriors, many against one, sent him to Yama's abode.
Other great chariot-warriors, surrounding an elephant and the best chariots, killed as they fled with a great cry the one armed with weapons.
Likewise elephants, O great king, surrounding on every side an enraged chariot-warrior scattering many arrows, killed him.
Elephant against elephant, chariot-warrior against chariot-warrior in the battle, able men killed each other here and there with javelins and iron arrows.
Chariots, elephants and horses crushing foot-soldiers were seen in the midst of the battle making great confusion.
Horses adorned with fly-whisks ran about like swans of the Himalaya as if drinking the earth.
The earth, varicoloured with the hooves of those horses, O lord of men, shone like a woman wounded by nail-marks.
With the sound of horses' hooves, of chariot wheel-rims, of foot-soldiers, and the trumpeting of elephants,
with the noise of instruments and the sound of conches, the earth resounded as if with thunderclaps, O Bharata.
With bows twanging, swords gleaming and the lustre of armour, nothing could be made out.
Many severed arms, like the trunks of elephant-kings, writhed and twisted, making dreadful motion.
The sound of heads falling to the ground, O great king, was heard like that of palm fruits dropping from trees.
The earth shone with fallen heads wet with blood, golden-hued, like lotuses in due season, O Bharata.
With those heads, eyes rolled, lifeless and deeply wounded, the earth shone, O great king, covered as with white lotuses.
With fallen arms anointed with sandal, with armlets, costly, the earth shone, O king of kings, like Indra's banners.
That battlefield was strewn with thighs of kings cut off in the great battle, like elephants' trunks.
Thronged with hundreds of headless trunks and adorned with parasols and fly-whisks, the forest of the army shone like a forest full of flowers.
The warriors there, O great king, ranging fearless, were seen with limbs smeared with blood like flowering kimshuka trees.
Elephants too were seen, tormented by arrows and javelins, falling here and there in the battle like cut clouds.
The elephant force, O great king, being slain by the great souls, scattered in all directions like clouds driven by wind.
Those cloud-like elephants fell on the earth on all sides, shining like mountains shattered by thunderbolts at the end of the age.
Heaps of horses with their riders fallen on the earth were seen everywhere like mountains.
On the battlefield a river arose bearing to the next world, with blood for water, whirlpools of chariots, banners as trees, bones as gravel,
arms as crocodiles, bows as currents, elephants as hills, horses as rocks, fat and marrow as mud, parasols as swans, maces as rafts,
covered with armour and turbans, with pennants as fair trees, bearing wheels as ruddy-geese, wrapped in triple poles and rods,
giving joy to the brave and increasing fear of the timid, a dreadful river flowed, thronged with Kurus and Srinjayas.
That very terrible river bearing to the world of the fathers, those heroes with arms like iron clubs crossed with their mounts as boats.
While the battle, O lord of men, went on without restraint, with the dreadful destruction of the four-limbed army, like the war of gods and asuras of old,
some cried out for their kinsmen here and there, scorcher of foes; with kinsmen crying out, others fled in fear and did not turn back.
While the unrestrained and terrible battle went on, Arjuna and Bhimasena bewildered the enemy.
That great army of yours, O lord of men, being slain, was bewildered there as women are by drink.
Having bewildered that army, Bhimasena and Dhananjaya blew their conches and roared lion-roars.
Hearing that great sound, Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin, putting the king of dharma before them, rushed at the king of the Madras.
There we saw a dreadful wonder, O lord of men: the heroes who met Shalya fought each by turns.
The two sons of Madri, impetuous, skilled in weapons and arrogant in battle, hastily attacked your army, wishing to conquer it.
Then your army, O best of the Bharatas, turned back, driven by many arrows from the victorious Pandavas.
That army of your sons, being slain in your sight, O great king, scattered in all directions, driven by firm bowmen, and a great cry of "Alas" arose among your warriors, O Bharata.
Stand, stand!—such was the cry of the great-souled kshatriyas fleeing, while each wished victory in the battle; and the Pandavas' men ran at your broken soldiers.
Leaving dear sons, brothers, grandfathers, maternal uncles, sisters' sons and relatives and kinsmen in the battle,
your warriors, urging horses and elephants, went in all directions, O best of the Bharatas, zealous for their own protection.
[Shalya said:] "There stands King Yudhishthira, son of Pandu, shining under his held white parasol.
Bring me quickly there, charioteer; see my strength; the Parthas are not able to stand before me in battle today."
Thus addressed, the king of the Madras' charioteer drove to where the king, true to his word, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, was.
As the great Pandava force came suddenly on, Shalya alone held it in the battle, as the shore holds back a raised ocean.
The flood of the Pandava force, O revered one, reaching Shalya, halted then in the battle like a river's rush at a mountain.
Seeing the king of the Madras ready for battle, the Kurus turned back, making death their return.
When they had turned back, O king, with their divisions arrayed in parts, a most dreadful battle with blood for water began; and Nakula, arrogant in battle, met Chitrasena.
Those two, meeting, holding variegated bows, were like two clouds risen, raining south and north.
They drenched each other with arrow-waters in the battle; I see no difference there between the Pandava and the other.
Both skilled in weapons, strong, adept in chariot-play, intent on slaying each other, each seeking the other's opening.
Chitrasena with a yellow, sharp broad-headed arrow cut Nakula's bow at the hand-grip, O great king.
Then, unflurried, he struck the bowless one on the forehead with three gold-feathered stone-whetted arrows.
He sent his horses to death with sharp arrows, and felled his banner and charioteer with three each.
Struck on the forehead by three arrows loosed from his foe's arm, Nakula shone, O king, like a mountain with three peaks.
With his bow cut and chariotless, the hero took sword and shield and descended from the chariot like a lion from a mountain peak.
As he rushed on foot, Chitrasena loosed a shower of arrows; Nakula, light-footed, took them on his shield.
Reaching Chitrasena's chariot, the varied fighter, free of weariness, the mighty-armed one mounted it in the sight of the whole army.
The Pandava cut off Chitrasena's head, with earrings and crown, fine nose and large eyes, from his body; it fell from the chariot seat, shining like the sun.
Seeing Chitrasena slain, the great chariot-warriors there raised cries of "Well done" and many lion-roars.
Seeing their brother slain, Karna's two sons, great chariot-warriors, Sushena and Satyasena, loosing sharp arrows,
then quickly ran at the Pandava, best of chariot-warriors, wishing to kill him as two tigers a great elephant in a forest, O king.
Those two keen warriors rushed at that great chariot-warrior, both showering floods of arrows like two clouds of water.
Pierced on all sides by arrows, the Pandava, as if delighted, took another bow, mounted the chariot and stood in the battle, the valiant hero, like enraged Death.
His two brothers, O king, began to shatter his chariot with straight-jointed arrows, O lord of men.
Then Nakula, laughing, killed Satyasena's four horses with four sharp arrows in the battle.
Then, fixing a gold-feathered, stone-whetted iron arrow, the Pandava cut Satyasena's bow, O king of kings.
Then mounting another chariot and taking another bow, Satyasena and Sushena rushed at the Pandava.
Madri's son, glorious, unflurried, pierced them both with two arrows each at the head of the battle, O great king.
Sushena, enraged, laughing, cut the Pandava's great bow in the battle with a razor-arrow, the great chariot-warrior.
Then Nakula, overcome with rage, taking another bow, pierced Sushena with five and cut his banner with one.
He swiftly cut Satyasena's bow and hand-guard in the battle, O revered one, and the people shouted.
Then, taking another bow, swift and able to bear weight, he covered the son of Pandu with arrows on every side.
Warding off those arrows, Nakula, slayer of heroes, pierced Satyasena and Sushena with two each.
They pierced him back separately with straight-flying arrows and struck his charioteer, O king of kings, with sharp arrows.
Satyasena, skilled-handed, glorious, cut Nakula's chariot-pole and bow, one by one, with two arrows.
Standing on his chariot, that atiratha took up a chariot-dart with a golden shaft, undulled tip, washed in oil and spotless,
like a licking great-venomous naga-maiden, lord; raising it, he hurled it at Satyasena in the battle.
It split his heart in a hundred ways in the fight, O king; he fell from the chariot to the ground, lifeless, barely conscious.
Seeing his brother slain, Sushena, overcome with rage, quickly showered the Pandava, who was on foot, with arrows.
Seeing Nakula chariotless, the mighty son of Draupadi, Sutasoma, rushed up, wishing to save his father in the battle.
Then Nakula, mounting Sutasoma's chariot, shone, best of the Bharatas, like a lion on a mountain; taking another bow, he fought Sushena.
Those two great chariot-warriors, meeting each other with showers of arrows, strove for each other's death.
Sushena, enraged, pierced the Pandava with three arrows and Sutasoma with twenty in arms and chest.
Then, enraged, O great king, Nakula, slayer of heroes, valiant, covered all his quarters with arrows.
Then, taking a sharp, keen half-moon arrow of great speed, he loosed it at Karna's son in the battle.
With it, O best of kings, he struck his head from his body in the sight of the whole army; it was as marvellous.
Slain by the great-souled Nakula, he fell, O king, like a great tree on a river bank torn by the current.
Seeing the slaying of Karna's son and Nakula's valour, your army, O best of the Bharatas, fled in fear.
That army the glorious king of the Madras, the brave commander, tamer of foes, protected in the battle.
Fearless, O great king, he stood, rallying the army, raising a loud lion-roar and the dreadful sound of his bow.
Your men, protected by the firm bowman, O king, advanced on the foes in the battle on all sides, free of distress.
Surrounding the mighty-bowed king of the Madras on all sides, the great army stood eager to fight, O king.
Satyaki, Bhimasena, the two sons of Madri and the Pandava, putting Yudhishthira, tamer of foes, in front,
surrounded him in the battle, the heroes, raising lion-roars, and made fierce sounds of arrows and various shouts.
Likewise all your men, surrounding the lord of the Madras with great vigour, again chose battle.
Then began the battle that increased the fear of the timid, of yours and the enemy, having made death their return.
As the battle of gods and asuras was of old, O lord of men, so this increased Yama's realm for the fearless, O king.
Then the monkey-bannered Pandava, O king, having slain the Samshaptakas in the battle, rushed at the Kaurava army.
Likewise the remaining Pandavas led by Dhrishtadyumna rushed at that army, loosing sharp arrows.
Scattered by the Pandavas, confusion arose; they knew neither the divisions nor the quarters and intermediate quarters.
Filled with sharp arrows driven by the Pandavas, its heroes slain, shattered and scattered on every side, the army was slain by the great chariot-warrior sons of Pandu, O Kaurava.
Likewise the Pandava army, O king, was struck on every side in the battle by your sons, by hundreds and thousands.
Those two armies, much scorched, being slain one by the other, became distraught like rivers in the rains.
Then a great and terrible fear entered yours and the Pandavas' men, O king of kings, in that great battle.
With the cries and groans of foot-soldiers in the great battle, with horses fleeing in many ways, O great king,
with dreadful destruction having come, the slaughter of all embodied beings, with weapons of many kinds heaped, chariots and elephants entangled,
with the joy of those eager for battle and the fear of the timid, with warriors plunging in, each wishing the other's death,
the taking of lives most dreadful going on, a gamble, the terrible battle that increased Yama's realm,
the Pandavas smote your army with sharp arrows, and likewise your warriors smote the Pandava soldiers.
While that fear-bringing battle for the timid went on, the forenoon having come, towards sunrise,
the enemy, having attained their aims and protected by the great soul, fought your force, having made death their return, O king.
By the strong, proud Pandavas who had attained their aims and were skilled strikers, your army sank, O Kaurava, like a doe surrounded by fire.
Seeing that army sinking like a weak cow in mud, Shalya, wishing to raise it, advanced against the Pandava host.
The king of the Madras, enraged, taking his excellent bow, rushed in the battle at the Pandavas, the aggressors.
And the Pandavas, O great king, victorious in the battle, reaching the king of the Madras, pierced him with sharp arrows.
Then the mighty king of the Madras with hundreds of sharp arrows tormented that army in the sight of the king of dharma.
Then, O king, many portents of various forms appeared, and the earth with its mountains trembled with a roar.
Meteors with staffs and spears, blazing at the tips, fell scattering from the sky to earth, striking the sun's disc.
Deer, buffaloes and birds, O lord of men, circled the army to the left again and again.
Then that fight of the band-ranging warriors became very fierce; all the divisions met, O lord of men, and the Kauravas, O king, advanced on the Pandava army.
Shalya, raining a shower of arrows like the thousand-eyed one, undaunted, showered the son of Kunti, Yudhishthira.
He also showered Bhimasena with gold-feathered stone-whetted arrows, and the sons of Draupadi and both sons of Madri.
The mighty one pierced Dhrishtadyumna, Shaineya and Shikhandin, each with ten arrows, and then loosed a shower of arrows like Maghavan at the end of summer.
Then thousands of Prabhadrakas and Somakas, O king, were seen fallen and falling from Shalya's arrows.
As swarms of bees, as flights of locusts, as hail from clouds, Shalya's arrows fell.
Elephants, horses, afflicted foot-soldiers and chariot-warriors fell, wandered and cried out from Shalya's arrows.
As if possessed by wrath and manliness, the lord of the Madras covered his foes in the battle like Time-sent Death; roaring, the lord of the Madras, thunder-voiced and mighty.
Slain by Shalya, the Pandava army rushed at Ajatashatru, Yudhishthira son of Kunti.
Having overwhelmed it in the battle, light-handed, with sharp arrows and a great shower of arrows, he tormented Yudhishthira.
As Shalya came on with foot-soldiers and horses, King Yudhishthira, enraged, held him back with sharp arrows, as one holds a rutting elephant with goads.
Shalya loosed at him a dreadful arrow like a venomous serpent; it pierced the great soul and fell swiftly to the earth.
Then Vrikodara, enraged, pierced Shalya with seven, Sahadeva with five, Nakula with ten arrows.
The sons of Draupadi showered the glorious slayer of foes, the brave Artayani, with arrows like clouds on a mountain.
Then, seeing Shalya being harassed on all sides by the Parthas, Kritavarman and Kripa, enraged, rushed up.
Uluka, Patri, Shakuni son of Subala, and Ashvatthaman the great chariot-warrior, smiling, slowly, and your sons all together protected Shalya in the battle.
Kritavarman, having pierced Bhimasena with three arrows, held him back with a great arrow-shower, enraged in form.
Kripa, enraged, tormented Dhrishtadyumna with arrows; Shakuni attacked the sons of Draupadi and Drona's son the twins.
Duryodhana, of fierce splendour, attacked in the battle Keshava and Arjuna, best of warriors, and the strong one struck them with arrows.
Thus hundreds of duels took place between yours and theirs, dreadful and varied, here and there, O lord of men.
Bhoja killed Bhima's brown horses in the battle; descending from the chariot seat, his horses slain, the son of Pandu, mace in hand, fought, raising it like Death's rod.
In front of Sahadeva the king of the Madras killed his horses; then Sahadeva killed Shalya's son with his sword.
Again the preceptor Gautama fought Dhrishtadyumna, calm against calm, effortful against more effortful.
The preceptor's son pierced the heroic sons of Draupadi, each with ten arrows, smiling as if not much angered.
Shalya too, O king, enraged, slaying the Somakas and Pandavas, again tormented Yudhishthira with sharp arrows.
Bhima, enraged in the battle, his lips bitten between his teeth, resolving on his destruction, valiant, took up his mace.
Like Death's rod, like the Night of Time raised up, the ender of lives of elephants, horses and men,
bound with plates of gold, like a blazing meteor, like a dreadful she-serpent in a net, like a thunderbolt, made of iron,
smeared with sandal and aguru paste, like a woman desired, smeared with fat, marrow and flesh, like Vaivasvata's tongue,
with hundreds of loud bells' sounds, like Indra's thunderbolt, like a shed serpent's coil, mingled with elephants' rut,
terrifying to enemy armies, delighting his own army, renowned in the world of men, splitting mountain peaks,
with which the strong son of Kunti, at Kailasa, challenged the enraged lord of Alaka, friend of Maheshvara,
with which, enraged, the mighty one slew many proud illusion-working guhyakas in Dhanada's abode, for the sake of the mandara flower, doing Draupadi's pleasure though held back by many.
Raising that mace, eight-edged, jewelled and heavy as a thunderbolt, the mighty-armed one rushed at Shalya in the battle.
Skilled in battle with the mace, with that dreadfully sounding mace he crushed Shalya's four very swift horses.
Then Shalya, enraged in the battle, drove a javelin into his broad chest, roaring, and piercing his armour it went in.
Vrikodara, our brother, pulling out that very javelin, pierced the charioteer of the king of the Madras in the heart with it.
With his armour split, vomiting blood, his mind terrified, the charioteer fell facing him, and the king of the Madras withdrew, dejected.
Seeing the act repaid with a return, Shalya, astonished in mind, taking his mace, the steadfast one, looked at his enemy.
Then the Parthas, glad at heart, honoured Bhimasena, seeing that dreadful deed of the unwearied-working one in the battle.
Bhima, taking a great mace, rushed with speed at him, who was blazing like the fire of destruction, like Death with noose in hand, like Kailasa with peaks, like Vasava with thunderbolt,
like a lion with a trident, like a rutting elephant in a forest.
Then the roar of conches and thousands of trumpets and a lion-roar arose that increased the joy of the brave.
Watching on all sides those two great elephants among warriors, the warriors of yours and the enemy said "Well done, well done."
For no one other than the lord of the Madras, or Rama, or the delight of the Yadus (Krishna), could bear Bhimasena's speed in battle.
And likewise none other than Vrikodara, among warriors, could bear the mace-speed of the great-souled lord of the Madras in the battle.
Roaring like bulls, those two ranged in circles, leaping, mace in hand, the lord of the Madras and Vrikodara.
In the circling paths and the sporting with maces, the fight between those two lions among men was without distinction.
Shalya's mace, with its bright plates of heated gold, became fearful, like struck by flames of fire.
Likewise Bhima's mace, as the great soul ranged in his paths and circles, shone like lightning in a cloud.
Sitting there around the banyan, grieving, they thought of that very matter that had passed—the destruction of the Kurus and Pandavas.
Out of fondness for your sons, wishing to do what was dear to him, O king, you have received this remorse afterwards; you ought not to grieve.
If I should make peace with Yudhishthira by your counsel, people will think me afraid of the white-horsed one in the battle.
Sighing slightly, the serpent, restraining himself with difficulty, pained by the noose, uttered a soft human voice.
Having said so much, Govinda, of great splendour, ceased; and Yudhishthira spoke to him.
When the days have been counted, at the shraddha for his sons, let the king give to all whatever he wishes.
A man, terrible, ugly, shaven, dark and tawny, having surveyed the houses of the Vrishnis, was not seen again anywhere.
Behind came the fair-hipped, dark, lotus-petal-eyed Draupadi, best of women, O best of the Bharatas.
Have those kings not gained this good imperishable world? I will not dwell without them, my kinsmen and brothers.
